claim: Endothelial cell (EC) activation is an early hallmark in the pathogenesis of chronic vascular diseases.
source: Endothelial cell (EC) activation is an early hallmark in the pathogenesis of chronic vascular diseases.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about vascular disease pathogenesis.

claim: MicroRNA-181b (Mir181b) is an important anti-inflammatory mediator in the vascular endothelium affecting endotoxemia, atherosclerosis, and insulin resistance.
source: MicroRNA-181b (Mir181b) is an important anti-inflammatory mediator in the vascular endothelium affecting endotoxemia, atherosclerosis, and insulin resistance.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by references to prior work.

claim: Methotrexate (MTX) and its downstream metabolite adenosine exert anti-inflammatory effects in the vascular endothelium by targeting and activating Mir181b expression.
source: Herein, we identify that the drug methotrexate (MTX) and its downstream metabolite adenosine exert anti-inflammatory effects in the vascular endothelium by targeting and activating Mir181b expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Both systemic and endothelial-specific Mir181a2b2-deficient mice develop vascular inflammation, white adipose tissue (WAT) inflammation, and insulin resistance in a diet-induced obesity model.
source: Both systemic and endothelial-specific Mir181a2b2-deficient mice develop vascular inflammation, white adipose tissue (WAT) inflammation, and insulin resistance in a diet-induced obesity model.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: MTX attenuated diet-induced WAT inflammation, insulin resistance, and EC activation in a Mir181a2b2-dependent manner.
source: Moreover, MTX attenuated diet-induced WAT inflammation, insulin resistance, and EC activation in a Mir181a2b2-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing loss of MTX effects in knockout mice.

claim: MTX attenuated cytokine-induced EC activation through a unique adenosine-adenosine receptor A3-SMAD3/4-Mir181b signaling cascade.
source: Mechanistically, MTX attenuated cytokine-induced EC activation through a unique adenosine-adenosine receptor A3-SMAD3/4-Mir181b signaling cascade.
evidence: This mechanistic claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Activated endothelial cells orchestrate the expression of adhesion molecules and release chemokines to foster the recruitment of leukocytes into the vessel wall.
source: Activated endothelial cells (ECs) orchestrate the expression of adhesion molecules and release chemokines to foster the recruitment of leukocytes into the vessel wall.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about EC function.

claim: EC activation contributes to the development of chronic vascular disease states, such as atherosclerosis, insulin resistance, and rheumatoid arthritis (RA).
source: This presents an early hallmark that contributes to the development of chronic vascular disease states, such as atherosclerosis, insulin resistance, and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) (Khan et al., 2010; Rao et al., 2007; Speyer and Ward, 2011; Sun et al., 2014a; MICU Registry et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Targeting EC activation and/or dysfunction may open new therapeutic approaches for the prevention and treatment of inflammatory diseases.
source: Accumulating studies demonstrate that targeting EC activation and/or dysfunction may open new therapeutic approaches for the prevention and treatment of inflammatory diseases (Chen et al., 2017; Gareus et al., 2008; Nus et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Inhibition of NF-κB activity specifically in the vascular endothelium significantly reduced atherosclerotic plaque formation and progression.
source: For example, inhibition of NF-κB activity specifically in the vascular endothelium significantly reduced atherosclerotic plaque formation and progression (Gareus et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are important post-transcriptional regulators of gene expression through mRNA degradation or translational repression.
source: MicroRNAs (miRNAs), a class of evolutionary conserved small non-coding RNAs, are important post-transcriptional regulators of gene expression through mRNA degradation or translational repression (Loyer et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about miRNA function, supported by citations.

claim: Mir181b prevents EC activation and diverse vascular inflammatory disease states including endotoxemia, atherosclerosis, insulin resistance, and arterial thrombosis.
source: We have previously identified microRNA-181b (Mir181b), an anti-inflammatory miRNA, which prevents EC activation and diverse vascular inflammatory disease states including endotoxemia, atherosclerosis, insulin resistance, and arterial thrombosis (Lin et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2014a; MICU Registry et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: Mir181b expression is significantly reduced in response to a range of pro-inflammatory stimuli in the vascular endothelium.
source: Mir181b expression is significantly reduced in response to a range of pro-inflammatory stimuli in the vascular endothelium (Lin et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2014a; MICU Registry et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Methotrexate (MTX) is a first-line treatment in RA and other autoimmune-mediated inflammatory diseases.
source: Methotrexate (MTX) is a first-line treatment in RA and other autoimmune-mediated inflammatory diseases.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about MTX use.

claim: Low-dose MTX could reduce cardiovascular risk in patients with RA.
source: Observational studies suggested that low-dose MTX could reduce cardiovascular risk in patients with RA (Charles-Schoeman et al., 2017; Deyab et al., 2017; Hjeltnes et al., 2013; Kisiel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to observational studies.

claim: The PSARA study demonstrated that patients receiving MTX improved endothelial function and reduced E-selectin plasma levels after 6 months follow-up.
source: For example, the Psoriatic arthritis, Ankylosing spondylitis, Rheumatoid Arthritis Study (PSARA) demonstrated that patients receiving MTX improved endothelial function and reduced E-selectin plasma levels after 6 months follow-up (Deyab et al., 2017; Hjeltnes et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the PSARA study.

claim: MTX treatment significantly lowered carotid intima-media thickness in RA patients compared to placebo.
source: Another clinical trial identified that MTX treatment significantly lowered carotid intima-media thickness in RA patients compared to placebo (Kisiel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a clinical trial.

claim: The CIRT trial found that low-dose MTX did not reduce cardiovascular events compared to placebo.
source: However, the recent Cardiovascular Inflammation Reduction Trial (CIRT), designed to determine the effect of low-dose MTX on cardiovascular secondary prevention, found that low-dose MTX did not reduce cardiovascular events compared to placebo (Ridker et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the CIRT trial.

claim: Adenosine has been identified as a potential metabolite activated in response to MTX in ECs.
source: While adenosine has been identified as a potential metabolite activated in response to MTX in ECs (Haskó and Cronstein, 2013), gaps remain in our understanding of the downstream signaling pathways underlying its effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: MTX (10 µM) but not statins significantly upregulated MIR181B expression by 1.35-fold in cultured human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs).
source: MTX (10 µM) but not statins significantly upregulated MIR181B expression by 1.35-fold in cultured human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The MTX-induced expression of MIR181B was dose- and time-dependent with the highest induction at 10 µM and 4 hr.
source: The MTX-induced expression of MIR181B was dose- and time-dependent with the highest induction at 10 µM and 4 hr (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: Adenosine is the major anti-inflammatory effector of MTX, which is a product of adenosine monophosphate, a reaction catalyzed by the enzyme ecto-5' nucleotidase.
source: Previous studies have established that adenosine (Ad) is the major anti-inflammatory effector of MTX, which is a product of adenosine monophosphate, a reaction catalyzed by the enzyme ecto-5' nucleotidase (Chan and Cronstein, 2013; Gadangi et al., 1996; Tian and Cronstein, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: When using a competitive enzyme inhibitor of ecto-5' nucleotidase (APCP), the MTX-induced MIR181B expression was completely blocked.
source: When using a competitive enzyme inhibitor of ecto-5' nucleotidase (α, β-methylene adenosine-5'-diphosphate (APCP)), the MTX-induced MIR181B expression was completely blocked (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Adenosine alone increased MIR181B expression in a dose- and time-dependent manner with the highest observed increase by 2.3-fold at 50 µM and 4 hr.
source: Conversely, Ad alone increased MIR181B expression in a dose- and time-dependent manner with the highest observed increase by 2.3-fold at 50 µM and 4 hr (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1E and 1F.

claim: ECs treated with MTX or Ad significantly reduced VCAM-1, ICAM-1, and E-selectin expression stimulated by TNF-α.
source: As expected, ECs treated with MTX or Ad significantly reduced VCAM-1, ICAM-1, and E-selectin expression stimulated by TNF-α (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Only primary transcript of the MIR181B-2 locus, and not primary MIR181B-1, MiR-181A-1, or MiR-181A-2, was rescued by MTX or Ad co-stimulation.
source: Only primary transcript of the MIR181B-2 locus, and not primary MIR181B-1, MiR-181A-1, or MiR-181A-2, was rescued by MTX or Ad co-stimulation (Figure 1H,I; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1H, 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: In ECs isolated from wild-type flox mice, MTX or Ad inhibited VCAM-1 protein expression by 40% and 35%, respectively.
source: In ECs isolated from wild-type flox mice, MTX or Ad inhibited VCAM-1 protein expression by 40% and 35%, respectively.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1J.

claim: MTX or Ad did not reduce VCAM-1 expression in primary ECs from Mir181a2b2—/— KO mice.
source: However, MTX or Ad did not reduce VCAM-1 expression in primary ECs from Mir181a2b2—/— KO mice (Figure 1J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Only silencing of ADORA3 reduced MIR181B basal expression by 40%, while knockdown of ADORA1, ADORA2A, and ADORA2B had no effect on MIR181B expression.
source: Only silencing of ADORA3 reduced MIR181B basal expression by 40%, while knockdown of ADORA1, ADORA2A, and ADORA2B had no effect on MIR181B expression (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Neither MTX nor Ad increased MIR181B expression in ADORA3-deficient HUVECs compared to negative control siRNA.
source: Indeed, neither MTX nor Ad increased MIR181B expression in ADORA3-deficient HUVECs compared to negative control siRNA (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Treatment of ECs with TNF-α in the presence of MTX or Ad rescued the TNF-α-mediated repression of MIR181B expression in an AdoRA3-specific manner.
source: Treatment of ECs with TNF-α in the presence of MTX or Ad rescued the TNF-α-mediated repression of MIR181B expression in an AdoRA3-specific manner (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Silencing of ADORA3 (and not ADORA1, ADORA2A, or ADORA2B) abrogated the anti-inflammatory effect of MTX or Ad in TNF-α-activated ECs on VCAM-1, ICAM-1, and E-Selection expression.
source: Furthermore, silencing of ADORA3, (and not ADORA1, ADORA2A, or ADORA2B) abrogated the anti-inflammatory effect of MTX or Ad in TNF-α-activated ECs on VCAM-1, ICAM-1, and E-Selection expression (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: While the MTX or Ad anti-inflammatory effects were blocked in the presence of ADORA3 silencing, overexpression of MIR181B fully rescued the MTX and Ad-mediated reduction of ECs activation markers.
source: While the MTX or Ad anti-inflammatory effects were blocked in the presence of ADORA3 silencing, overexpression of MIR181B fully rescued the MTX and Ad-mediated reduction of ECs activation markers (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: MTX and Ad activated the −606 bp MIR181A2B2 promoter reporter construct from 1.47- to 1.57-fold, respectively.
source: MTX and Ad activated the −606 bp MIR181A2B2 promoter reporter construct from 1.47- to 1.57-fold, respectively (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A-B.

claim: Treatment of MTX or Ad similarly activated the −402 bp reporter comparable to the full-length constructs.
source: Treatment of MTX or Ad similarly activated the −402 bp reporter comparable to the full-length constructs (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Reducing the promoter length to −301 bp or −150 bp significantly reduced luciferase activity from 30- to 2600-fold, respectively.
source: However, reducing the promoter length to −301 bp or −150 bp significantly reduced luciferase activity from 30- to 2600-fold, respectively (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: MTX significantly increased pri-MIR181B-2 transcript stability, while Ad had a modest opposite effect.
source: However, MTX significantly increased pri-MIR181B-2 transcript stability, while Ad had a modest opposite effect (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Silencing of SMAD3 or SMAD4 reduced luciferase activity of the full length −606 bp construct by 37% and 42%, respectively, in ECs compared to control siRNA.
source: Silencing of SMAD3 or SMAD4 reduced luciferase activity of the full length −606 bp construct by 37% and 42%, respectively, in ECs compared to control siRNA (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: SMAD2 silencing did not impact luciferase activity.
source: However, SMAD2 silencing did not impact luciferase activity (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: MIR181B expression was significantly reduced only by silencing SMAD3 or SMAD4, and not by SMAD2 knockdown.
source: Consistent with this observation, MIR181B expression was significantly reduced only by silencing SMAD3 or SMAD4, and not by SMAD2 knockdown (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Silencing of SMAD3 or SMAD4 completely blocked the MTX and Ad-mediated increase in MIR181B expression.
source: Importantly, silencing of SMAD3 or SMAD4 completely blocked the MTX and Ad-mediated increase in MIR181B expression (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Knockdown ADORA3 blocked the MIR181A2B2 promoter luciferase activity induced by MTX and Ad.
source: Furthermore, knockdown ADORA3 blocked the MIR181A2B2 promoter luciferase activity induced by MTX and Ad (Figure 3F)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Silencing of the other three Ad receptors had no effect on luciferase activity.
source: however, silencing of the other three Ad receptors had no effect on luciferase activity (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Low-dose (i.e. 0.25 mg/kg) MTX showed no significant increase in Mir181b expression in plasma, liver, and intima, but 1 mg/kg did.
source: Low-dose (i.e. 0.25 mg/kg) MTX showed no significant increase in Mir181b expression in plasma, liver, and intima, but 1 mg/kg did (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: C57Bl6 mice treated with adenosine exhibited significantly elevated Mir181b expression in plasma by 168% and was even more pronounced than high-dose MTX.
source: Moreover, C57Bl6 mice treated with adenosine exhibited significantly elevated Mir181b expression in plasma by 168% and was even more pronounced than high-dose MTX (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The body weights among the four groups (flox and KO mice with or without MTX) were not significantly different.
source: As shown in Figure 4B, the body weights among the four groups were not significantly different, which suggest that the gain of body weight was independent of Mir181a2b2 expression and MTX treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: MTX treatment significantly improved insulin sensitivity and reduced the area under curves (AUC) for ITT by 23% compared with vehicle injected flox mice.
source: However, MTX treatment significantly improved insulin sensitivity and reduced the area under curves (AUC) for ITT by 23% (Figure 4C) compared with vehicle injected flox mice
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: MTX treatment did not improve glucose tolerance in flox mice.
source: but not in glucose tolerance (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: KO mice developed insulin resistance as shown by improved insulin sensitivity (increased AUC for ITT by 121%) and glucose tolerance (increased AUC GTT by 122%).
source: In line with our previous report showing a protective effect of Mir181b mimics on insulin resistance (Sun et al., 2016), KO mice developed insulin resistance (IR) as shown by improved insulin sensitivity (increased AUC for ITT by 121%) and glucose tolerance (increased AUC GTT by 122%) (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: The beneficial effect of MTX on insulin sensitivity was completely blocked in KO mice.
source: Notably, the beneficial effect of MTX on insulin sensitivity was completely blocked in KO mice (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: Flox mice treated with MTX had increased insulin signaling activity in eWAT and liver compared vehicle injected, indicated by an increase in phosphorylation of Akt (phospho-Akt) in eWAT (by 23%) and in liver (by 34%).
source: Moreover, flox mice treated with MTX had increased insulin signaling activity in eWAT and liver compared vehicle injected, indicated by an increase in phosphorylation of Akt (phospho-Akt) in eWAT (by 23%) and in liver (by 34%) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: KO mice without MTX injections showed a significant reduction of Akt phosphorylation by 24% in eWAT and 44% in liver compared with control flox mice.
source: In contrast, KO mice without MTX injections showed a significant reduction of Akt phosphorylation by 24% in eWAT and 44% in liver compared with control flox mice (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The MTX-mediated upregulation of phospho-Akt in eWAT and liver was blocked in KO mice.
source: Moreover, the MTX-mediated upregulation of phospho-Akt in eWAT and liver was blocked in KO mice (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: MTX did not increase phospho-Akt levels in skeletal muscle (SM).
source: However, MTX did not increase phospho-Akt levels in skeletal muscle (SM) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The most statistically significant altered genes in eWAT from Mir181a2b2 KO mice were linked to cell adhesion, chemotaxis, and immune response.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) suggested that the most statistically significant [false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.5] altered genes in eWAT from Mir181a2b2 KO mice were linked to cell adhesion (e.g. platelet-endothelium-leukocyte interactions, cell-matrix interactions, and cell junctions), chemotaxis, and immune response (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data and GSEA shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: In eWAT from MTX-treated Mir181a2b2 flox and KO mice, GSEA found that cell cycle, inflammation, and chemotaxis pathways were more affected by MTX.
source: In eWAT from MTX-treated Mir181a2b2 flox and KO mice, GSEA found that cell cycle, inflammation, and chemotaxis pathways were more affected by MTX (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C-D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data and GSEA shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C-D.

claim: MTX administration reduced VCAM-1 mRNA expression by 36% in eWAT in flox mice, but not MTX-injected KO mice.
source: Moreover, we confirmed that MTX administration reduced VCAM-1 mRNA expression by 36% in eWAT in flox mice, but not MTX-injected KO mice (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4F and 4G.

claim: Macrophage content, as indicated by Mac2 staining, was significantly reduced by 80% in eWAT in MTX-injected flox mice.
source: In line with reduced VCAM-1 expression, we observed that macrophage content, as indicated by Mac2 staining, was significantly reduced by 80% in eWAT in MTX-injected flox mice (Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: KO mice treated with MTX showed no inhibitory effect on VCAM-1 mRNA expression and macrophage content in eWAT.
source: In contrast, KO mice treated with MTX showed no inhibitory effect on VCAM-1 mRNA expression and macrophage content in eWAT (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4F and 4G.

claim: Mir181b expression in tamoxifen injected iEC-KO mice was reduced by 60% and 80% in aortic intima and ECs isolated from SM, respectively, but not in the aortic media and non-EC fraction of SM.
source: Compared to vehicle control injected mice, Mir181b expression in tamoxifen injected iEC-KO mice was reduced by 60% and 80% in aortic intima and ECs isolated from SM, respectively, but not in the aortic media and non-EC fraction of SM (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–E.

claim: While Mir181b was reduced in the aortic intima of iEC-KO mice compared to flox-Cre, MTX increased Mir181b in flox-Cre, but not in iEC-KO mice.
source: While Mir181b was reduced in the aortic intima of iEC-KO mice compared to flox-Cre, MTX increased Mir181b in flox-Cre, but not in iEC-KO mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: MTX reduced VCAM-1 expression in the intima of flox-Cre mice, but not in iEC-KO mice.
source: Consistent with upregulated Mir181b expression, MTX reduced VCAM-1 expression in the intima of flox-Cre mice, but not in iEC-KO mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: SMAD2 and SMAD3 expression decreased in MTX-treated iEC-KO mice compared to flox-Cre mice.
source: We found that SMAD2 and SMAD3 expression decreased in MTX-treated iEC-KO mice compared to flox-Cre mice, whereas there were no differences between flox-Cre and iEC-KO mice without MTX treatment, suggesting a feedback mechanism involved in the MTX-SMAD-Mir181b cascade (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: There were no significant differences in body weights between iEC-KO and control mice treated with or without MTX after 12 weeks of HFD.
source: As shown in Figure 5B, there were no significant differences in body weights between iEC-KO and control mice treated with or without MTX after 12 weeks of HFD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: MTX administration significantly improved insulin sensitivity by 23% in ITT of control flox-Cre mice.
source: However, MTX administration significantly improved insulin sensitivity by 23% in ITT of control flox-Cre mice (Figure 5C)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: MTX had no effect on insulin sensitivity in iEC-KO mice.
source: whereas MTX had no effect on insulin sensitivity in iEC-KO mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: MTX administration did not improve glucose tolerance either in iEC-KO or control mice.
source: Similar to Mir181a2b2 systemic KO and control mice, MTX administration did not improve glucose tolerance either in iEC-KO or control mice (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The MTX-mediated induction of Akt phosphorylation in eWATs and livers was blocked in iEC-KO mice.
source: Moreover, the MTX-mediated induction of Akt phosphorylation in eWATs and livers was blocked in iEC-KO mice (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: MTX reduced VCAM-1 expression in eWAT in flox-Cre control mice, but not in iEC-KO mice.
source: Furthermore, MTX reduced VCAM-1 expression in eWAT in flox-Cre control mice, but not in iEC-KO mice (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: MTX administration significantly reduced Mac2 positive macrophage content in eWAT tissues in flox-Cre mice, whereas no effect was observed in iEC-KO mice.
source: Consistent with previous results (Figure 4H), MTX administration significantly reduced Mac2 positive macrophage content in eWAT tissues in flox-Cre mice, whereas no effect was observed in iEC-KO mice (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: iEC-KO mice without MTX treatment showed a significant increase in Mac2 positive macrophages compared to flox-Cre control mice in eWAT tissues.
source: Finally, iEC-KO mice without MTX treatment showed a significant increase in Mac2 positive macrophages compared to flox-Cre control mice in eWAT tissues (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Low-grade inflammation in adipose tissue plays a critical role in the pathogenesis of obesity-associated insulin resistance.
source: Low-grade inflammation in adipose tissue plays a critical role in the pathogenesis of obesity-associated insulin resistance, an important risk factor for the development of cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes (Arner and Kulyté, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The CANTOS trial demonstrated that targeting inflammation reduces cardiovascular events by targeting interleukin-1β, independent of lipid lowering.
source: The Canakinumab Atherosclerosis Outcome Thrombosis Study (CANTOS) demonstrated that targeting inflammation reduces cardiovascular events by targeting interleukin-1β, independent of lipid lowering (Ridker et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the CANTOS trial.

claim: MTX did not reduce inflammatory markers, such as interleukin-1, interleukin-6, C-reactive protein, or cardiovascular events in the CIRT trail.
source: In contrast, MTX, an anti-inflammatory drug that is widely used to treat patients with RA and psoriatic arthritis, did not reduce inflammatory markers, such as interleukin-1, interleukin-6, C-reactive protein, or cardiovascular events in the CIRT trail (Ridker et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the CIRT trial.

claim: By decreasing the catabolism of adenosine, MTX increases extracellular Ad, which in turn mediates its cellular effects via engagement of specific receptors (A1, A2A, A2B, and A3).
source: By decreasing the catabolism of adenosine, MTX increases extracellular Ad, which in turn mediates its cellular effects via engagement of specific receptors (A1, A2A, A2B, and A3; Cronstein and Sitkovsky, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Among adenosine receptors, A2A and A3 are the most important receptors for mediating adenosine's cellular anti-inflammatory effect.
source: Among these adenosine receptors, A2A and A3 are the most important receptors for mediating adenosine's cellular anti-inflammatory effect (Cronstein et al., 1993; Montesinos et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Mir181b expression was reduced by 40–60% in the vascular endothelium under atherosclerosis, sepsis, thrombosis, insulin resistance, and other conditions.
source: For instance, we and others found that Mir181b expression was reduced by 40–60% in the vascular endothelium under atherosclerosis, sepsis, thrombosis, insulin resistance, and other conditions (Guo et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2014a; MICU Registry et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Overexpression of Mir181b by tail vein injection of Mir181b mimics (~1.5- to 2.5-fold increase in Mir181b expression) improved acute vascular inflammation induced by endotoxemia.
source: Overexpression of Mir181b by tail vein injection of Mir181b mimics (~1.5- to 2.5-fold increase in Mir181b expression) improved acute vascular inflammation induced by endotoxemia (MICU Registry et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Overexpression of Mir181b improved chronic vascular inflammation triggered by atherosclerotic plaque formation.
source: and chronic vascular inflammation triggered by atherosclerotic plaque formation (Sun et al., 2014a)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Overexpression of Mir181b improved obesity and insulin resistance.
source: obesity and insulin resistance (Sun et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Overexpression of Mir181b improved thrombin-induced arterial thrombosis.
source: and thrombin-induced arterial thrombosis (Lin et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In ECs, Mir181b inhibits NF-κB signaling by targeting importin-α3 or caspase recruitment domain family member 10 (Card10).
source: In ECs, Mir181b inhibits NF-κB signaling by targeting importin-α3 or caspase recruitment domain family member 10 (Card10), whereas it activates phospho-Akt by targeting, pleckstrin homology domain leucine-rich repeat protein phosphatase isozyme2 (PHLPP2) (Lin et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2014a; MICU Registry et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mir181b activates phospho-Akt by targeting pleckstrin homology domain leucine-rich repeat protein phosphatase isozyme2 (PHLPP2).
source: In ECs, Mir181b inhibits NF-κB signaling by targeting importin-α3 or caspase recruitment domain family member 10 (Card10), whereas it activates phospho-Akt by targeting, pleckstrin homology domain leucine-rich repeat protein phosphatase isozyme2 (PHLPP2) (Lin et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2014a; MICU Registry et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Using an E-selectin-targeting microparticles system to deliver Mir181b specifically to the activated vascular endothelium, Mir181b significantly reduced atherosclerosis.
source: Moreover, using an E-selectin-targeting microparticles system to deliver Mir181b specifically to the activated vascular endothelium, Mir181b significantly reduced atherosclerosis (Ma et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Ad is continuously released by cells to the extracellular environment at a low concentration (less than 1 µM) in unstressed tissues.
source: Ad is continuously released by cells to the extracellular environment at a low concentration (less than 1 µM) in unstressed tissues, whereas Ad concentrations can reach as high as 100 µM in inflamed or ischemic tissues (Haskó and Cronstein, 2004; Jacobson and Gao, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Ad concentrations can reach as high as 100 µM in inflamed or ischemic tissues.
source: Ad is continuously released by cells to the extracellular environment at a low concentration (less than 1 µM) in unstressed tissues, whereas Ad concentrations can reach as high as 100 µM in inflamed or ischemic tissues (Haskó and Cronstein, 2004; Jacobson and Gao, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ECs are a major source of extracellular Ad at sites of metabolic distress, inflammation, and infection.
source: In addition, ECs are a major source of extracellular Ad at sites of metabolic distress, inflammation, and infection (Cronstein, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Ad potently repressed TNF-α-induced inflammatory genes expression in an ADORA3-dependent manner, but not the other three Ad receptors.
source: In agreement with a recently published report (Xu et al., 2017), we found that Ad potently repressed TNF-α-induced inflammatory genes expression in an ADORA3-dependent manner, but not the other three Ad receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to a recent report.

claim: The MTX and Ad-mediated protective effects on ECs were dependent on Mir181b expression.
source: Moreover, we demonstrated that the MTX and Ad-mediated protective effects on ECs were dependent on Mir181b expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Silencing ADORA3 decreased Mir181b expression, and blocked the TNF-α-mediated repression of Mir181b expression and abrogated the MTX- and Ad-mediated induction of Mir181b expression.
source: Interestingly, silencing ADORA3 decreased Mir181b expression, and blocked the TNF-α-mediated repression of Mir181b expression and abrogated the MTX- and Ad-mediated induction of Mir181b expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: After TNF-α stimulation, the expression of adenosine kinase (ADK), a major intracellular adenosine metabolic enzyme, is increased and thereby results in decreased intracellular adenosine concentration, which in turn reduces extracellular adenosine.
source: Indeed, after TNF-α stimulation, the expression of adenosine kinase (ADK), a major intracellular adenosine metabolic enzyme, is increased and thereby results in decreased intracellular adenosine concentration, which in turn reduces extracellular adenosine (Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Systemic MiR181a2b2 KO and endothelial-specific-deficient Mir181a2b2 mice exhibited EC activation, vascular inflammation, and insulin resistance in obese mice.
source: Systemic MiR181a2b2 KO and endothelial-specific-deficient Mir181a2b2 mice exhibited EC activation, vascular inflammation, and insulin resistance in obese mice, suggesting that endothelial Mir181a2b2 plays a key role in EC activation and progression of insulin resistance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The anti-inflammatory effects and improvement in insulin sensitivity by MTX were dependent on endothelial Mir181a2b2.
source: Moreover, the anti-inflammatory effects and improvement in insulin sensitivity by MTX were dependent on endothelial Mir181a2b2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: MTX activated an Ad-ADORA3-SMAD3/4 signaling cascade that transcriptionally activated MIR181A2B2 expression and modestly increased pri-MIR181B2 mRNA stability at the post-transcriptional level.
source: Mechanistically, MTX activated an Ad-ADORA3-SMAD3/4 signaling cascade that transcriptionally activated MIR181A2B2 expression and modestly increased pri-MIR181B2 mRNA stability at the post-transcriptional level.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: High-dose of MTX (1 mg/kg) is essential to increase Mir181b expression and modulate a large gene network involving EC-leukocyte adhesion, chemotaxis, immune response, and cell cycle in eWAT.

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mir181a2b2 KO mice exhibited more glucose intolerance under basal conditions compared to flox mice, and this response was further exacerbated by MTX treatment.

claim: Systemic delivery of Mir181b mimics (to overexpress Mir181b) improved insulin resistance and increased phospho-AKT in eWAT but not in liver or skeletal muscle in HFD-induced obese mice.

claim: MTX treatment potently increased phospho-Akt in liver, eWAT, and skeletal muscle in control mice, but not in those tissues from Mir181a2b2—/— mice or in liver or eWAT in iECKO mice.

claim: Systemic double knockout of Mir181a1b1 and Mir181a2b2 improved HFD-induced obesity and insulin resistance.
